Louis XIV was born on 5 September 1638 in the [Château de Saint-Germain-en-Laye](/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_de_Saint-Germain-en-Laye "Château de Saint-Germain-en-Laye"), to [Louis XIII](/wiki/Louis_XIII "Louis XIII") and [Anne of Austria](/wiki/Anne_of_Austria "Anne of Austria"). He was named Louis Dieudonné (Louis the God-given)[[4]](#cite_note-6) and bore the traditional title of French [heirs apparent](/wiki/Heir_apparent "Heir apparent"): *[Dauphin](/wiki/Dauphin_of_France "Dauphin of France")*.[[5]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBluche199011-7) At the time of his birth, his parents had been married for 23 years. His mother had experienced four [stillbirths](/wiki/Stillbirth "Stillbirth") between 1619 and 1631. Leading contemporaries thus regarded him as a divine gift and his birth a miracle.[[6]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarentine2016129-8)

Louis' relationship with his mother was uncommonly affectionate for the time. Contemporaries and eyewitnesses claimed that the Queen would spend all her time with Louis.[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPanhuysen201626-9) Both were greatly interested in food and theatre. This long-lasting and loving relationship can be evidenced by excerpts in Louis' journal entries, such as:

> Nature was responsible for the first knots which tied me to my mother. But attachments formed later by shared qualities of the spirit are far more difficult to break than those formed merely by blood.[[8]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFraser200614–16-10)

In 1975, Faust joined the [University of Pennsylvania](/wiki/University_of_Pennsylvania "University of Pennsylvania") faculty as assistant professor of American civilization. Her area of specialty was the history of the South during the [antebellum](/wiki/Antebellum_era "Antebellum era") period and the [Civil War](/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War"). She rose to become [Walter Annenberg](/wiki/Walter_Annenberg "Walter Annenberg") Professor of History.

After publishing her thesis in book form as *A Sacred Circle: Dilemma of the Intellectual in the Old South, 1840-1860* (1977), she authored a series of non-fiction books on U.S. history. Among them was *James Henry Hammond and the Old South* (1982), a biography of [James Henry Hammond](/wiki/James_Henry_Hammond "James Henry Hammond"), Governor of South Carolina from 1842 to 1844. She followed that with *Mothers of Invention: Women of the Slaveholding South in the American Civil War* (1996), for which she won the [Society of American Historians](/wiki/Society_of_American_Historians "Society of American Historians") [Francis Parkman Prize](/wiki/Francis_Parkman_Prize "Francis Parkman Prize") and the [Avery O. Craven](/wiki/Avery_O._Craven "Avery O. Craven") Award from the [Organization of American Historians](/wiki/Organization_of_American_Historians "Organization of American Historians") in 1997. Her book *This Republic of Suffering* (2008) was a critically acclaimed exploration of how Americans' understanding of death was shaped by the high casualties during the Civil War.[[12]](#cite_note-12) It was a finalist for the [Pulitzer Prize](/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize_for_History "Pulitzer Prize for History") and [National Book Award](/wiki/National_Book_Award_for_Nonfiction "National Book Award for Nonfiction").

Brandy Clark was born in [Morton, Washington](/wiki/Morton,_Washington "Morton, Washington"), a logging town of 900 people in the shadow of [Mount Rainier](/wiki/Mount_Rainier "Mount Rainier"). As a child in the 1980s she was influenced by the country-pop and traditional country music artists she heard her parents and grandmother play, like [Barbara Mandrell](/wiki/Barbara_Mandrell "Barbara Mandrell"), [Ronnie Milsap](/wiki/Ronnie_Milsap "Ronnie Milsap"), [Merle Haggard](/wiki/Merle_Haggard "Merle Haggard") and [Loretta Lynn](/wiki/Loretta_Lynn "Loretta Lynn"). Clark cites the [Patsy Cline](/wiki/Patsy_Cline "Patsy Cline") biopic *[Sweet Dreams](/wiki/Sweet_Dreams_(1985_film) "Sweet Dreams (1985 film)")* as one of her biggest early influences.[[4]](#cite_note-CMT_Edge_Article-4)

Clark began playing guitar at nine years old and sang in school musicals, also writing songs. She obtained a basketball scholarship at [Central Washington University](/wiki/Central_Washington_University "Central Washington University"), but later moved back home, obtaining an associate degree from [Centralia College](/wiki/Centralia_College "Centralia College") in 1997. Still a teenager, she joined the music business program at [Belmont University](/wiki/Belmont_University "Belmont University"), and moved to Nashville in 1998.[[5]](#cite_note-CCFHG-5)
At Belmont she took guitar lessons again and joined a band with her mother and a friend. She studied commercial music and was chosen to perform in the school's "Best of the Best Showcase". Upon graduation, Clark got a job with Leadership Music which led to her eventual publishing deal.

[Alexander J. Davis](/wiki/Alexander_J._Davis "Alexander J. Davis")'s original designs for the university featured the Gothic Revival style. He is generally credited with coining the term "[Collegiate Gothic](/wiki/Collegiate_Gothic "Collegiate Gothic")"

Following Michigan's admission to the Union in 1837, an organic act was passed on March 18, 1837, to reorganize the university under a twelve-member board of regents.[[52]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShaw194232-56) The regents met in [Ann Arbor](/wiki/Ann_Arbor "Ann Arbor") and accepted the town's proposal for the university to relocate to Judge [Henry Rumsey](/wiki/Henry_Rumsey "Henry Rumsey")'s farmland.[[52]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShaw194232-56)

The approved campus plans for the university were drawn up by the architect [Alexander Davis](/wiki/Alexander_Jackson_Davis "Alexander Jackson Davis").[[53]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETruettner20031,_9-57)[[54]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMayer2015-58) Davis designed an elaborate [Gothic](/wiki/Gothic_architecture "Gothic architecture") main building with a large lawn in front, wide avenues, and botanical gardens, all arranged to evoke the French *[château](/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau "Château")* aesthetic.[[53]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETruettner20031,_9-57) He also provided possible sites for future buildings; however, the plans were never executed. Instead, four houses for professors were authorized. fanoutqa_004460.t: The Beatles :: History :: 1956–1963: Formation :: The Quarrymen and name changes :: chunk_0003
fanoutqa_004460.x:
The Beatles :: History :: 1956–1963: Formation :: The Quarrymen and name changes :: chunk_0003
Main article: [The Quarrymen](/wiki/The_Quarrymen "The Quarrymen")

In November 1956, sixteen-year-old [John Lennon](/wiki/John_Lennon "John Lennon") formed a [skiffle](/wiki/Skiffle "Skiffle") group with several friends from [Quarry Bank High School](/wiki/Quarry_Bank_High_School "Quarry Bank High School") in [Liverpool](/wiki/Liverpool "Liverpool"). They were called *[the Quarrymen](/wiki/The_Quarrymen "The Quarrymen")*, a reference to their school song "Quarry men old before our birth".[[10]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELewisohn2013104-10) Fifteen-year-old [Paul McCartney](/wiki/Paul_McCartney "Paul McCartney") met Lennon on 6 July 1957 and joined as a [rhythm guitarist](/wiki/Rhythm_guitar "Rhythm guitar") shortly after.[[11]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESpitz200593–99-11) In February 1958, McCartney invited his friend [George Harrison](/wiki/George_Harrison "George Harrison"), then aged fifteen, to watch the band. Harrison auditioned for Lennon, impressing him with his playing, but Lennon initially thought Harrison was too young. After a month's persistence, during a second meeting (arranged by McCartney), Harrison performed the lead guitar part of the instrumental song "[Raunchy](/wiki/Raunchy_(instrumental) "Raunchy (instrumental)")" on the upper deck of a Liverpool bus,[[12]](#cite_note-12) and they enlisted him as [lead guitarist](/wiki/Lead_guitar "Lead guitar").[[13]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles199747-13)[[14]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELewisohn199213-14)

By January 1959, Lennon's Quarry Bank friends had left the group and he began his studies at the [Liverpool College of Art](/wiki/Liverpool_College_of_Art "Liverpool College of Art").[[15]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarry2000a103-15) The three guitarists, billing themselves as Johnny and the Moondogs,[[16]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELewisohn199217-16) were playing [rock and roll](/wiki/Rock_and_roll "Rock and roll") whenever they could find a drummer.

For the first time since [2000](/wiki/2000_NBA_Playoffs "2000 NBA Playoffs"), the Miami Heat and the New York Knicks met in the postseason, reigniting the [Heat–Knicks rivalry](/wiki/Heat%E2%80%93Knicks_rivalry "Heat–Knicks rivalry").

For the fourth time since 2006, a division winner (in this case the [Atlantic Division](/wiki/Atlantic_Division_(NBA) "Atlantic Division (NBA)") champion [Boston Celtics](/wiki/Boston_Celtics "Boston Celtics")) opened the playoffs on the road. Despite not having home court advantage, the Boston Celtics beat the Atlanta Hawks in six games. The Hawks would not open the playoffs at home again until [2015](/wiki/2015_NBA_playoffs "2015 NBA playoffs").

Game 1 of the Bulls–Sixers series was extremely notable as [Derrick Rose](/wiki/Derrick_Rose "Derrick Rose") tore his ACL in the waning minutes of the Bulls’ 103–91 victory.

With their Game 3 loss to the Miami Heat, the [New York Knicks](/wiki/New_York_Knicks "New York Knicks") lost their 13th straight playoff game, breaking Memphis' record from 2004 to 2006 for the longest playoff losing streak. However, they broke that streak with a Game 4 victory against The Heat at [Madison Square Garden](/wiki/Madison_Square_Garden "Madison Square Garden").

With their Game 4 loss to the Oklahoma City Thunder, the defending champions [Dallas Mavericks](/wiki/Dallas_Mavericks "Dallas Mavericks") were swept in the first round, becoming the third defending champion to be swept in the First Round after the [Philadelphia Warriors](/wiki/Philadelphia_Warriors "Philadelphia Warriors") in [1957](/wiki/1957_NBA_playoffs "1957 NBA playoffs") and [Miami Heat](/wiki/Miami_Heat "Miami Heat") in [2007](/wiki/2007_NBA_playoffs "2007 NBA playoffs"), and second after Miami to be done so in a seven-game series. Daniil Medvedev :: part 02 :: chunk_0001
**Daniil Sergeyevich Medvedev**[[a]](#cite_note-5) (born 11 February 1996) is a Russian professional [tennis](/wiki/Tennis "Tennis") player. He has been ranked as the [world No. 1](/wiki/List_of_ATP_number_1_ranked_singles_tennis_players "List of ATP number 1 ranked singles tennis players") in men's singles by the [Association of Tennis Professionals](/wiki/Association_of_Tennis_Professionals "Association of Tennis Professionals") (ATP). Medvedev has won 23 [ATP Tour](/wiki/ATP_Tour "ATP Tour")-level singles titles, including the [2021 US Open](/wiki/2021_US_Open_%E2%80%93_Men%27s_singles "2021 US Open – Men's singles") and [2020 ATP Finals](/wiki/2020_ATP_Finals_%E2%80%93_Singles "2020 ATP Finals – Singles").

Medvedev made his ATP Tour main draw debut at the [2015 Kremlin Cup](/wiki/2015_Kremlin_Cup_%E2%80%93_Men%27s_doubles "2015 Kremlin Cup – Men's doubles"). In 2018, Medvedev won his first three ATP Tour singles titles. He had a breakthrough year in 2019, making his top 10 debut and reaching six consecutive tournament finals, including the [US Open](/wiki/2019_US_Open_%E2%80%93_Men%27s_singles "2019 US Open – Men's singles").[[5]](#cite_note-6) In 2020 Medvedev won the [ATP Finals](/wiki/2020_ATP_Finals_%E2%80%93_Singles "2020 ATP Finals – Singles"), defeating the top three players in the world en route to the title.[[6]](#cite_note-7) In 2021, he contested his second and third [major](/wiki/Grand_Slam_(tennis)#Tournaments "Grand Slam (tennis)") finals, and won the [US Open](/wiki/2021_US_Open_%E2%80%93_Men%27s_singles "2021 US Open – Men's singles") to claim his first major title and deny [Novak Djokovic](/wiki/Novak_Djokovic "Novak Djokovic") a [Grand Slam](/wiki/Grand_Slam_(tennis) "Grand Slam (tennis)").[[7]](#cite_note-8) He also helped the [Russian Davis Cup team](/wiki/Russia_Davis_Cup_team "Russia Davis Cup team") secure victory in [2021](/wiki/2021_Davis_Cup_Finals "2021 Davis Cup Finals").[[8]](#cite_note-9)

fanoutqa_013676.x:
São Paulo :: Geography :: Climate :: part 01 :: chunk_0018
[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a8/Tempestade_em_SP.jpg/250px-Tempestade_em_SP.jpg)](/wiki/File:Tempestade_em_SP.jpg)

Heavy rain and lightning in São Paulo, which has one of the largest number of [lightning](/wiki/Lightning "Lightning") incidents amongst Brazilian state capitals[[85]](#cite_note-85)

São Paulo features a [humid subtropical climate](/wiki/Humid_subtropical_climate "Humid subtropical climate") ([Köppen](/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification"): *Cwa*, [Trewartha](/wiki/Trewartha_climate_classification "Trewartha climate classification"): *Cwal*).[[86]](#cite_note-Climate-86) In summer (January through March), the mean low temperature is about 19 °C (66 °F) and the mean high temperatures is near 28 °C (82 °F). In winter, temperatures tend to range between 12 and 22 °C (54 and 72 °F). The record high temperature was 38.4 °C (101.1 °F) on 17 October 2014[[87]](#cite_note-bdmep.inmet.gov.br-87) and the lowest −3.2 °C (26.2 °F) on 25 June 1918.[[88]](#cite_note-88)[[89]](#cite_note-89) The highest accumulated rainfall in 24 hours was 151.8 mm (5.98 in) on December 21, 1988, followed by 144.1 mm (5.67 in) on January 25, 2025, and 140.4 mm (5.53 in) on May 25, 2005.[[87]](#cite_note-bdmep.inmet.gov.br-87)

The [Tropic of Capricorn](/wiki/Tropic_of_Capricorn "Tropic of Capricorn"), at about 23°27' S, passes through north of São Paulo and roughly marks the boundary between the tropical and [temperate](/wiki/Temperateness "Temperateness") areas of South America. Because of its elevation, however, São Paulo experiences a more temperate climate.[[90]](#cite_note-90) The summer is hot and rainy. Autumn and spring are transitional seasons. Winter is mild, but still the coldest season, with cloudiness around town and frequent polar air masses. Amongst the oldest evidence for human presence in South America is the [Monte Verde II](/wiki/Monte_Verde "Monte Verde") site in Chile, suggested to date to around 14,500 years ago.[[16]](#cite_note-27) From around 13,000 years ago, the [Fishtail projectile point](/wiki/Fishtail_projectile_point "Fishtail projectile point") style became widespread across South America, with its disappearance around 11,000 years ago coincident with the disappearance of South America's megafauna.[[17]](#cite_note-:12-28) Maize was present in northern South America by around 6,000 years ago.[[18]](#cite_note-29)

Denmark national football team :: History :: The Møller Nielsen fairytale: 1992 European Championship :: chunk_0006
Denmark began Euro 1992 qualification with a home victory against the [Faroe Islands](/wiki/Faroe_Islands_national_football_team "Faroe Islands national football team"), and followed up with an away draw against [Northern Ireland](/wiki/Northern_Ireland_national_football_team "Northern Ireland national football team") and a 2–0 home loss against [Yugoslavia](/wiki/Yugoslavia_national_football_team "Yugoslavia national football team"). Brothers [Michael Laudrup](/wiki/Michael_Laudrup "Michael Laudrup") and [Brian Laudrup](/wiki/Brian_Laudrup "Brian Laudrup") opted to quit the national team in November 1990. When Nielsen subsequently decided to dismiss quality players such as [Jan Mølby](/wiki/Jan_M%C3%B8lby "Jan Mølby") and [Jan Heintze](/wiki/Jan_Heintze "Jan Heintze") from the squad due to disciplinary problems, several newspapers began demanding that Nielsen step down as head coach. Despite this, Denmark won the rest of their five matches in the qualification group, including a 2–1 away win against Yugoslavia. This was not enough to qualify, as the team still had to settle for second place in the group, behind Yugoslavia.[[14]](#cite_note-14)

Due to international sanctions resulting from the [Yugoslav wars](/wiki/Yugoslav_wars "Yugoslav wars"), [UEFA](/wiki/UEFA "UEFA") announced on 31 May 1992 – only 10 days before the competition – that [Yugoslavia](/wiki/Yugoslavia "Yugoslavia") was excluded from the competition and their place given to Denmark, who finished as the second-placed team in its qualifying group.[[15]](#cite_note-15)[[16]](#cite_note-16)[[17]](#cite_note-17)[[18]](#cite_note-18)
